requirements.how_to_verify: The register holds 39 sources, three added on 2026-09-22: `npm` (registry search, GET /-/v1/search, documented at https://github.com/npm/registry/blob/main/docs/REGISTRY-API.md), `npm_downloads` (GET /downloads/point/{period}, documented at https://github.com/npm/registry/blob/main/docs/download-counts.md) and `pypi` (the two RSS feeds the operator directs consumers to, documented at https://docs.pypi.org/api/feeds/). Each carries the operator's own rate-limit or data-limit text quoted with the date it was read, in `rate_limit_note`. Run `python3 -c "from selflearn.fetch.registry import registry_summary; print(registry_summary())"` for the counts and `python3 -m unittest tests.test_access_policy.AdapterRouteTests -v` for the routes each adapter builds. npm search and both PyPI feeds were polled live on 2026-09-22 and returned 10 items each.

requirements.gap: Matching is against the path only, not the query string: RFC 9309 2.2.2 speaks of the path while its Figure 4 lists a URL with a query under a column headed 'Path to Match', which is ambiguous. The departure is recorded in the module docstring and on the sources page. In this sandbox most hosts are unreachable, so their recorded status is `unreachable_disallowed` - an honest description of no egress, not a statement about the operator; CI regenerates the table from a runner with unrestricted egress.
requirements.how_to_verify: `selflearn/fetch/robots.py` implements RFC 9309 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html) clause by clause, each rule citing the clause that requires it: group selection by product-token substring and `*` fallback (2.2.1), most-specific-match-by-octets with allow winning ties (2.2.2), `#`, `$` and `*` (2.2.3), a 4xx robots.txt failing open (2.3.1.3), an unreachable one failing closed (2.3.1.4), a 24-hour cache (2.4) and a 512 KiB parsing limit (2.5). The gate is attached to the HTTP client, so no caller can bypass it. Run `python3 -m selflearn robots` for every route the engine would request with the verbatim rule behind each decision, or `python3 -m unittest tests.test_access_policy -v` for the 31 offline cases. The published site carries the same rows at `docs/sources.html#policy`. PyPI is the case that decided the design: https://pypi.org/robots.txt (fetched 2026-09-22) disallows "/pypi/*/json" and "/search*" to every user agent, so the engine requests only the RSS feeds the operator's own API page recommends.

requirements.gap: The sweep proves a request can be built and that its route is the operator's documented one; it does not prove the response parses, which needs a live response. requirements.how_to_verify: Asking all 39 adapters to build their requests for one ordinary research query found two that could not. `worldbank` interpolated nothing into "/country/all/indicator/{indicator}" and raised `KeyError: 'indicator'`; it is replaced by `WorldBankSource`, which uses only the routes the operator documents at https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/898599-indicator-api-queries (read 2026-09-22): /v2/indicator for all indicators and /v2/indicator/<code> for one, with ?format=json. `eurostat` interpolated the prose query into the dataset path, which can only answer 404; it now uses a documented dataset unless the query already is a dataset code. Run `python3 -m unittest tests.test_access_policy.AdapterRouteTests.test_every_registered_adapter_can_build_a_request -v`, which is that sweep as a regression test.

robots.txt","maintainers":[{"name":"tomgco","email":"tomgallacher23@gmail.com"},{"name":"balaclark","email":"balaclark@gmail.com"}],"readme":"## Robots.txt

Pass in the location of your `robots.txt` file on the file system, and this module
will return you a piece of Connect/Express middleware that will serve it at `GET /robots.txt`.

This makes one *synchronous* call to read the file upon start up, then reads it from memory
for every request. If you gave the wrong path, you will know about it at startup. Cache headers
are set for you.

## Installation

    npm install --save robots.txt

## Usage

    var robots = require('robots.txt')

    // Pass in the absolute path to your robots.txt file
    app.use(robots(__dirname + '/robots.txt'))

## Credits
Built by [Tom Gallacher](http://twitter.com/tomgco) and [Ben Gourley](https://github.com/bengourley)

## Licence

robots.txt","maintainers":[{"name":"tomgco","email":"tomgallacher23@gmail.com"},{"name":"balaclark","email":"balaclark@gmail.com"}],"readme":"## Robots.txt

Pass in the location of your `robots.txt` file on the file system, and this module
will return you a piece of Connect/Express middleware that will serve it at `GET /robots.txt`.

This makes one *synchronous* call to read the file upon start up, then reads it from memory
for every request. If you gave the wrong path, you will know about it at startup. Cache headers
are set for you.

## Installation

    npm install --save robots.txt

## Usage

    var robots = require('robots.txt')

    // Pass in the absolute path to your robots.txt file
    app.use(robots(__dirname + '/robots.txt'))

## Credits
Built by [Tom Gallacher](http://twitter.com/tomgco) and [Ben Gourley](https://github.com/bengourley)

## Licence

matrix.license_name: Package metadata as published by each package's own maintainers
matrix.name: npm Registry Search API
matrix.notes: Search results carry the registry's own ranking; `score.detail.quality`, `score.detail.popularity` and `score.detail.maintenance` are the operator's figures, not this engine's. A package description is the maintainer's own text and is quoted as such. Access policy: https://registry.npmjs.org/robots.txt answered HTTP 200 on 2026-09-22 with content-type application/json - the package document of an npm package literally named 'robots.txt', not a robots file. It contains no user-agent lines, so under RFC 9309 2.2.1 no rules apply and the engine may request the documented search route. The observation is published on the sources page rather than resolved silently.
matrix.rate_limit_note: The operator publishes no numeric request limit for the public registry API. The documentation directory of npm/registry was listed on 2026-09-22 (COUCHDB.md, REGISTRY-API.md, REPLICATE-API.md, download-counts.md, follower.md, restful-api-conventions.md, varnish-config.md, hooks/, orgs/, responses/, user/) and contains no rate-limit document; the 2017 announcement that introduced registry rate limiting now carries the operator's own notice that 'The content in this blog post is no longer applicable/has been deprecated' (https://blog.npmjs.org/post/164799520460/api-rate-limiting-rolling-out.html, read 2026-09-22). Two documented limits are honoured: REGISTRY-API.md gives the search parameter `size` a default of 20 and a maximum of 250, and the same announcement states that package search queries must be at least three characters long. HTTP 429 is treated as retryable and recorded.

matrix.license_name: Aggregate download statistics published by the registry operator
matrix.name: npm Download Counts API
matrix.notes: Counts are the operator's own daily aggregation of install logs, not a live figure. download-counts.md states (read 2026-09-22): 'npm's raw log data is continuously written to a series of buckets on AWS S3. Once per day, soon after UTC midnight, a map-reduce cluster is spun up that crunches the previous day's logs and pushes them into the database.' Every claim from this source is therefore about a closed day or period, and the `start` and `end` dates the API returns are quoted with the count.
matrix.rate_limit_note: Documented data limits, quoted from download-counts.md (read 2026-09-22): 'Bulk queries are limited to at most *128* packages at a time and at most *365 days* of data.' and 'All other queries are limited to at most *18 months* of data. The earliest date for which data will be returned is January 10, 2015.' No requests-per-hour figure is published; HTTP 429 is treated as retryable and recorded.

matrix.license_name: Project names, summaries and descriptions supplied by each project's own uploaders
matrix.name: PyPI RSS Feeds (newest packages and latest updates)
matrix.notes: Access policy, stated in full because it decided the route: https://pypi.org/robots.txt (fetched 2026-09-22) disallows '/pypi/*/json', '/pypi/*/*/json', '/pypi*?', '/search*', '/simple/' and '/packages/' to every user agent, so the JSON API documented at https://docs.pypi.org/api/json/ and the Index API at https://docs.pypi.org/api/index-api/ are not requested; the engine's RFC 9309 gate refuses them and publishes the rule that matched. '/rss/' is not disallowed, and the operator's own API policy page directs consumers there: 'For periodically checking for new packages or updates to existing packages, use our RSS feeds.' This source therefore reads the two documented global feeds, and the Project Releases Feed is available per project at https://pypi.org/rss/project/<project_name>/releases.xml.
matrix.rate_limit_note: Quoted from the operator's API policy page https://docs.pypi.org/api/ (read 2026-09-22): 'Due to the heavy caching and CDN use, there is currently no rate limiting of PyPI APIs at the edge.' The same page asks consumers to 'Set your consumer's `User-Agent` header to uniquely identify your requests' and to 'Try not to make a lot of requests (thousands) in a short amount of time (minutes)'. The Terms of Service API Terms (effective February 25, 2025) add that 'Abuse or excessively frequent requests to PyPI via the API may result in the temporary or permanent suspension of your Account's access to the API.' This engine asks for two feed documents per cycle.

experiments.hypothesis: On a 5-armed Bernoulli bandit with fixed means over 4000 pulls, UCB1 and epsilon-greedy (epsilon=0.1) both accumulate less pseudo-regret than round-robin, UCB1's regret grows sublinearly, and a fixed exploration rate keeps paying a cost proportional to the horizon.
experiments.method: 100 independent trials of 4000 pulls per policy on arms with means [0.15, 0.25, 0.35, 0.45, 0.6]; pseudo-regret computed from the true mean of each pulled arm, so the metric has no reward noise.

checks.check: round-robin pseudo-regret equals the analytic value T x mean gap
UCB1 accumulates less pseudo-regret than round-robin
epsilon-greedy accumulates less pseudo-regret than round-robin
UCB1 regret is sublinear: the second half of the horizon costs less than the first
a fixed exploration rate keeps paying: epsilon-greedy second-half regret stays above half its analytic floor

result_json.conclusion: hypothesis supported by all stated checks
result_json.falsifier: Round-robin is not the worst of the three, or UCB1's second-half regret is not below its first-half regret, or epsilon-greedy's second-half regret falls below the analytic exploration floor.
